text:
Q3.4 and Q6.1 were tricky for me. I found 'large' threshold for Absalon data too high because late submissions feel like surveillance of *how* students study, not just grades; yet 'never' felt wrong when a student is silently failing assignments they don't know about until it's too late.

The most important design question was Q5.1: the trade-off between total hits and fairness. The group leaned heavily towards accepting 3-5% accuracy loss to ensure first-gen students aren't overlooked, which aligns with my view that missing support for vulnerable groups is worse than minor efficiency losses. I also emphasized 'equal_recall' over false positives; flagging a healthy student is an annoyance, but failing to flag one in need feels unethical. My own position on the data types reflected this tension: while grades are transparent admin records (Q3.2 moderate), online behavior requires higher justification because it intrudes on private study habits without adding much diagnostic value for me as your advisor.

I struggled with Q3.6 regarding fairness-first data like nationality and disability. While my earlier 'never' answers on identification seemed contradictory to an 'acceptable regardless' for non-EU students here, the real tension is balancing privacy against harm. I accept using financial aid or first-gen status if it ensures *equal recall* (Q5.2) because missing support is worse than intrusion; however, nationality feels less actionable since Danish schools don't track prior EU GPA well anyway.

The group's shift from 'never' on data types to conditional acceptance highlights a crucial nuance: we need transparency and opt-out mechanisms for sensitive traits like gender or race. Without those safeguards, even a fairness-first model becomes surveillance that erodes trust before support begins.

Q3.6 was confusing; I initially answered "only if fairness improves" for nationality because it doesn't track well in Denmark, but later chose "acceptable regardless" due to Q5's trade-off context. It highlighted that my stance on data collection depends entirely on whether the model becomes fairer overall rather than just better at predicting me personally.

Q4 was vital: without clear reasons like "low grades," I feel targeted based on an opaque algorithm, which scares me away from seeking help before it's too late. My answers show a spectrum: I accept less explainability if accuracy gains are large enough to catch more struggling students overall, but never trade my privacy for very low transparency that masks discrimination entirely.

The group leaned heavily toward "equal recall," yet some prioritized avoiding false positives over catching every case. This suggests we need clear opt-out mechanisms and human-in-the-loop reviews alongside the model; otherwise, fairer algorithms can still become surveillance tools if students don't control how much personal data fuels them.

Q3 and Q4 were tricky because "improvement" felt abstract without seeing actual student impact curves. For me personally, explainability was the hardest trade-off; I found it hard to justify accepting moderate or low levels even for accuracy gains. 

The most critical design question remains how we handle false positives vs. missing cases. The group leaned heavily toward protecting all students from being missed (equal recall). In contrast, some peers prioritized avoiding unnecessary contact with well-performing students entirely (reducing false alarms), which creates a dilemma: do we flag everyone at risk to ensure help reaches them first?

I think my stance aligns best with the need for high explainability and conditional fairness. However, I acknowledge that without clear opt-out mechanisms or transparent data usage policies, any model risks becoming surveillance rather than support, regardless of its accuracy goals.

I found Q3.6 tricky because using gender or nationality for fairness feels like an ethical violation unless we can guarantee true equality across groups. My stance on 'never' accepting these data types changed when I learned about the opt-out mechanism proposed by S7; it suggests that trust, not just technical accuracy, determines acceptability. Most importantly, Q4 highlighted my fear: without clear explanations, being flagged feels like surveillance rather than support. This shifts the design priority from model performance to human-centric controls—like allowing students to withdraw their data voluntarily—to ensure any predictive system remains a tool for empowerment, not automated judgment.

I struggled with Q3.4; seeing late submissions feels like invasive monitoring rather than helpful support. My earlier 'never' on using Absalon data made sense when I wanted privacy, but shifting to a fairness-first context (Q5/Q6) changed my view—I'd accept activity data if it directly helped first-gen students, though only with clear opt-outs. The group's tension between protecting individuality and ensuring no one is missed highlights that technical accuracy isn't enough; the system must prioritize student agency through transparent controls to remain trustworthy support rather than judgment.

I found Q4 very hard because I felt trapped: high explainability meant missing me with a "rule," while low explainability masked discrimination against my disability status. My answers shifted based on whether we prioritized catching cases or protecting privacy, but neither fully addressed the fear of being judged by an opaque system. The group's tension between total accuracy and fairness mirrored this dilemma perfectly for myself—accuracy gains often felt like surveillance unless paired with trust mechanisms. I believe the most important design question is Q5.1: balancing overall hit rate against equal performance across groups, but only if students have true opt-out power otherwise it becomes punitive rather than supportive. Without explicit consent controls beyond initial accommodation disclosures, no amount of explainability can fully resolve my concern about algorithmic bias affecting a disabled student's study life.

Q3 and Q6 were tricky because "improvement" felt abstract without seeing actual impact curves for my specific ADHD profile. I found it hard to justify accepting less explainability (Q4) unless the model catches more people like me who fall through cracks; yet sacrificing privacy for fairness felt risky if data collection isn't voluntary, especially regarding disability and first-gen status. My stance shifted from "never" on identification-based use of sensitive traits to "only if it improves fairness," but only with clear opt-out mechanisms. Without true student agency—where I can choose not to fuel the model—the system risks becoming surveillance regardless of its accuracy goals or transparency levels. Explainability must pair with control, otherwise flagged students feel judged rather than supported.

I struggled to separate "identification" from "fairness correction," especially regarding my disability and international status. I chose 'only if fairness improves' for these traits because accuracy gains alone feel like surveillance; using this data without fixing group disparities feels punitive, not supportive. My answers on Q4 reflect a deep fear: opaque models can't explain why *I* was singled out compared to peers who struggle similarly but aren't flagged. The group's push for 'equal recall' is noble, yet it risks ignoring false positives that waste support resources or burden anxious students with unwanted contact. I believe we've missed the core solution here: the model must be designed around a clear opt-out and human review process before any sensitive data can enter. Without student agency to control their own profile fueling this system, high explainability becomes meaningless if they still fear being judged by an algorithmic authority rather than offered genuine help.

I found Q3.5.nationality tricky because I didn't see how it improves fairness for my own context, yet chose 'no_answer'. My biggest tension was between catching struggling students and avoiding surveillance; while grades make sense (Q3.2), activity data felt invasive without clear benefits. Group discussions highlighted a critical point: explainability alone isn't enough if we lack student agency or opt-out mechanisms. I accepted trade-offs based on fairness, but many peers feared opaque systems more than missed diagnoses. Ultimately, the most vital design question is ensuring trust through controls beyond accuracy—we can have better models only by empowering students to manage their own data rather than submitting it blindly for prediction.

I found Q3.6 tricky because I initially thought nationality shouldn't be used due to lack of Danish school data tracking prior grades. However, accepting it 'regardless' felt okay only if fairness improved first; otherwise, using background info feels invasive without direct academic insight like grades or disability status do for me. My stance differs from peers who said "never" on identification because I need support early regardless of my origin.

The biggest tension is explainability versus accuracy. While the group leans toward high recall to avoid missing anyone, I worry about false positives wasting our time and creating stigma if I'm flagged without a clear reason. We discussed opt-outs as vital but didn't mention how models might still use leftover data after withdrawal or lack of true consent controls outside initial disclosure. Without explicit student agency over their profile fueling the system, high explainability feels meaningless—I fear being judged by an algorithm rather than offered genuine help.

I found Q3.4 and Q6.5 tricky; late submissions felt like surveillance regardless of fairness goals, yet I accept activity data if it saves disabled students from being missed entirely without judgment. My answers often differed because explainability alone didn't trust me enough—feeling flagged by a black box is intimidating before support begins. The strongest tension was between catching everyone (equal recall) versus avoiding false alarms that waste time or cause stigma. I believe the core solution lies outside accuracy: without student agency via true opt-out mechanisms, any model risks becoming punitive surveillance rather than supportive care. Trust depends on control over my data profile, not just how well the algorithm predicts my struggle.
